section_summary: This section contains State Department records from July through September 1938 concerning internal Japanese economic policy and Japanese military interference with American rights, properties, and citizens during the Second Sino-Japanese War. A major topic is the wartime economic program of Finance Minister Seihin Ikeda, who instituted autonomous trade councils and linked raw material import allocations directly to manufactured exports to conserve foreign exchange. The bulk of the section comprises Tokyo Embassy Despatch No. 3081 and its enclosures, documenting Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's formal representations of July 4, 1938, to Japanese Foreign Minister Kazushige Ugaki regarding the Open Door, extraterritoriality, aerial bombings, and widespread assaults on American nationals. Transmitted with the despatch is an extensive 23-page itemized compilation detailing hundreds of incidents of destruction, seizure, and violence against American missions, hospitals, schools, commercial assets, and diplomatic properties across China since July 1937, including the atrocities in Nanking.

subfiles.about: Continuation of a telegram detailing Ambassador Grew's oral representations to Foreign Minister Ugaki and Ugaki's responses regarding American rights and Japanese military actions in China.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart (relaying Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.summary: Concluding pages of Grew's July 4, 1938 conference with Ugaki, raising property and treaty rights and incidents. Ugaki pledges peace, the Open Door and no indiscriminate bombing, blaming damage on poorly trained aviators.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 945 from Shanghai relaying Tokyo Telegram No. 427: Ambassador Grew's Representations to Japanese Foreign Minister Ugaki

subfiles.about: Telegram informing Ambassador Grew of Secretary Hull's replies at a press conference concerning reports of the Grew-Ugaki conference on American rights in China.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Grew that at a July 6 press conference he confirmed receiving a report of the Ugaki meeting, reached no conclusions, and said international law governs claims.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 231 to American Embassy, Tokyo: Press Conference Inquiries Regarding Representations on American Rights in China

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet recording Ambassador Grew's Despatch No. 2972 regarding a conversation with German industrialist Edmund Stinnes on the liquidation of world dictatorships.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 2972 (793.94/13252): Grew's conversation with Edmund Stinnes, who urged liquidating the Italian, Japanese and German dictatorships as the best contribution to peace.
subfiles.title: Document File Note for Tokyo Despatch No. 2972: Conversation between Ambassador Grew and Edmund Stinnes

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum analyzing Japanese Finance Minister Seihin Ikeda's trade and exchange policies and import-export control amendments.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Despatches 3000 and 3032: Ikeda's trade reforms give industrial guilds enforcement and link import quotas to exports; gold shipment planned. Japan's economy likely permanently altered along fascist lines.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Finance Minister Ikeda's Policies and Import-Export Control Amendment

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the economic policies and structural trade reforms introduced by Japan's Minister of Finance and of Commerce and Industry, Seihin Ikeda.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew analyzes the economic program formulated by Seihin Ikeda upon assuming the concurrent portfolios of Finance and Commerce and Industry. Seeking to alleviate business dissatisfaction caused by rigid, hastily organized governmental trade restrictions since September 1937, Ikeda proposed delegating administrative responsibility to organized, autonomous industry councils and traditional trade associations. He advocated linking import allowances of scarce raw materials directly to export performance, curbing domestic consumption through savings campaigns, and discouraging exports to yen-currency areas like Manchuria and North China to preserve non-yen foreign exchange. Grew concludes that while these policies rely on traditional Japanese commercial groupings, they reflect a broader reorganization that will leave Japan's economic structure permanently transformed along fascist corporatist lines.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3000: Finance Minister Ikeda's Policies

subfiles.about: Cover memorandum and routing slip submitting the record and digest of Ambassador Grew's July 4 interview with Foreign Minister Ugaki to the Secretary of State and the Legal Adviser.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck sends Hull Grew's July 4, 1938 Ugaki conference record, with a Far Eastern digest of Despatch No. 3081; routing slip asks that the file go to Mr. Matre.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Adviser on Political Relations Hornbeck Transmitting Digest of Despatch No. 3081, with Legal Adviser Routing Slip

subfiles.about: Internal Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing the key points of Tokyo Despatch No. 3081 concerning Ambassador Grew's interview with Foreign Minister Ugaki.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury (Division of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Salisbury digests Despatch No. 3081: Japanese claims of Chinese military use of mission property, Ugaki's complaint about American magazine articles on the Imperial Household, and extraterritoriality statements. He recommends reading it all.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum: Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 3081 on Ambassador Grew's Interview with Foreign Minister Ugaki
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck / Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting the full record of conversation, written representations, itemized incident list, and Japanese notes regarding Ambassador Grew's interview of July 4, 1938, with Foreign Minister Ugaki.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a detailed official record of his crucial conference on July 4, 1938, with Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs General Kazushige Ugaki concerning American rights and interests affected by hostilities in China. The despatch includes four extensive enclosures: a comprehensive 11-page memorandum of conversation detailing discussions on extraterritoriality, local settlements, press criticisms of the Imperial Household, and the destruction of salvaged Standard Oil vessels; the informal written statement of representations left with Ugaki along with an appended letter protesting the aerial bombing of a Baptist mission school in Pingtu, Shantung; a 23-page itemized compilation of hundreds of incidents across China since July 1937 involving Japanese bombing, shelling, seizure, and looting of American properties, violent assaults on American citizens, and extensive atrocities committed during the occupation of Nanking; and an English translation of Foreign Minister Ugaki's reference notes setting forth Japanese military justifications and alleging Chinese militarization of mission compounds.
subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 3081: American Property and Interests in China; Ambassador Grew's Interview with the Minister for Foreign Affairs (with Enclosures 1-4)
